plan.chapterName: OpenStax Calculus, chapter 12: Vectors in Space
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a three-dimensional construction drawn in the first octant that locates a single point three different ways at once. The vertical axis is labeled z, the axis running to the right is labeled y, and the axis coming toward the viewer at the lower left is labeled x. A filled black dot at the upper right is tagged by two stacked lines of text, P(x, y, z) on top and P(rho, theta, phi) beneath it. A solid blue segment runs from the origin out to the dot and is labeled rho along its length. A small arc near the origin between the z-axis and that segment is labeled phi. Dashed orange lines complete the rest of the construction: a vertical drop from the point down to the xy-plane labeled z, and a segment from the origin across the xy-plane to the foot of that drop labeled r, with a small square where they meet marking the right angle. A second arc at the origin, between the x-axis and the segment r, is labeled theta. Superimposing all three descriptions on one point exposes theta and r as the quantities the systems share. The drawing introduces the ordered triple (rho, theta, phi), in which one distance and two angles fix a location in space.

elements: z-axis: vertical line through origin with arrowhead at top, label 'z'
y-axis: line from origin toward screen-right (slightly down) with arrowhead, label 'y'
x-axis: line from origin toward screen lower-left (out of page) with arrowhead, label 'x'
origin point where the three axes meet
point P: filled black dot in the first octant (upper-right region)
stacked text labels at P: 'P(x, y, z)' on top line and 'P(ρ, θ, φ)' beneath
solid blue radial segment from origin to P, labeled 'ρ' at its midpoint
angle arc φ near origin between the +z-axis and the ρ segment, labeled 'φ'
dashed orange vertical segment dropping from P straight down to its foot on the xy-plane, labeled 'z'
foot point on the xy-plane directly below P
dashed orange segment from origin across the xy-plane to the foot, labeled 'r'
small right-angle square marker at the foot between the r-direction and the vertical z-direction
angle arc θ at origin in the xy-plane between the +x-axis and the r segment, labeled 'θ'

interactions.teaches: Rotating the construction confirms P is a single fixed location in 3D space; the dashed drop and ground segment reveal its height above and footprint within the xy-plane

interactions.label: ρ (radius)
interactions.teaches: ρ is the straight-line distance from the origin to P; increasing it slides P outward along the same ray while both angles stay fixed

interactions.label: θ (azimuth)
interactions.teaches: θ is the angle in the xy-plane measured from the +x-axis to the ground projection r; sweeping it rotates P around the z-axis at constant height

interactions.label: φ (polar)
interactions.teaches: φ is the angle down from the +z-axis to the radial segment ρ; increasing φ tilts P away from the vertical, lowering z and lengthening the ground radius r

interactions.label: Coordinate readout
interactions.teaches: The same point P is described three ways; toggling highlights which quantities are shared (θ and the vertical height appear in cylindrical, r and θ in the ground plane) and which are unique to each system

demo_steps.title: Spherical default
demo_steps.narration: With ρ=2.5, θ=45°, φ=55° the blue radial segment, the φ arc from the z-axis, the dashed ground radius r with its θ arc, and the vertical drop z all locate one point P.

demo_steps.title: Tilt down with φ
demo_steps.narration: Raise φ to 80°: P swings toward the xy-plane, the vertical z shrinks and the ground radius r grows — φ alone controls elevation.

demo_steps.title: Rotate with θ
demo_steps.narration: Set θ to 15°: P rotates about the z-axis while ρ, φ and the height z stay unchanged — θ only changes the compass direction of the footprint.

demo_steps.title: Compare readouts
demo_steps.narration: Switch the readout to Rectangular: the identical point is now given as (x, y, z), making clear that z is shared with cylindrical while x and y replace r and θ.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World scale: each axis spans ~3 units from the origin. Use spherical-to-Cartesian mapping x = ρ·sinφ·cosθ, y = ρ·sinφ·sinθ, z = ρ·cosφ (φ measured from +z, θ from +x toward +y). Default ρ=2.5, θ=45°, φ=55° places P in the upper-right first octant matching the source. Axis orientation in world space: +Y screen-up = z-axis, +X screen-right ≈ y-axis, +Z out-of-page toward lower-left ≈ x-axis (standard isometric pose handles this). Colors: axes dark grey #333333 with black arrowheads and labels; radial ρ segment solid blue #1a5fb4 with blue 'ρ' label; dashed construction lines orange #e8722a (vertical z drop, ground r segment, right-angle square); φ and θ angle arcs thin black #222222; point P black filled sphere ~0.07 radius; stacked P labels black. φ arc lies in the vertical plane containing the z-axis and P; θ arc lies flat in the xy-plane; right-angle marker is a small ~0.15-unit square at the foot in the vertical plane spanned by the r-direction and the vertical. Foot point = (x, y, 0).
interactionPlan.notes: Recompute P, the foot point, the ρ line, the dashed z and r segments, the right-angle square, and both angle arcs on every slider change. Build the φ arc as a sampled arc in the plane through +z and the ρ direction (radius ~0.5), and the θ arc as a sampled arc in the xy-plane from +x to the r direction (radius ~0.6). For the coordinate-readout toggle, keep all geometry in the scene and instead swap/emphasize the on-screen numeric triple and recolor the relevant segments: Rectangular highlights x,y,z (color the vertical drop and add x,y ground components), Cylindrical highlights r,θ,z, Spherical highlights ρ,θ,φ. Use dashed LineDashedMaterial (call computeLineDistances) for the orange construction lines. Labels rendered as sprites or CSS2D so they always face the camera and stay legible under orbit.

authoredContext:
In the spherical coordinate system, a point P in space (the figure) is represented by the ordered triple (ρ,θ,φ) where

In the Cartesian coordinate system, the location of a point in space is described using an ordered triple in which each coordinate represents a distance. In the cylindrical coordinate system, location of a point in space is described using two distances (randz) and an angle measure (θ). In the spherical coordinate system, we again use an ordered triple to describe the location of a point in space. In this case, the triple describes one distance and two angles. Spherical coordinates make it simple to describe a sphere, just as cylindrical coordinates make it easy to describe a cylinder. Grid lines for spherical coordinates are based on angle measures, like those for polar coordinates.

The relationship among spherical, rectangular, and cylindrical coordinates.

This figure is the first quadrant of the 3-dimensional coordinate system. It has a point labeled “(x, y, z) = (rho, theta, phi).” There is a line segment from the origin to the point. It is labeled “rho.” The angle between this line segment and the z-axis is phi. There is a line segment in the x y-plane from the origin to the shadow of the point. This segment is labeled “r.” The angle between the x-axis and r is theta.

By convention, the origin is represented as (0,0,0) in spherical coordinates.
